newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada Prairies hog output to rise on Asian demand.
newsitem.headline: Canada Prairies hog output to rise on Asian demand.

text.p: Hog production on Canada's Prairies should rise in response to growing Asian demand for high quality pork products, Canadian pork industry officials said.

"The western Canadian industry seems poised for some good, solid, sustained growth. There's lots of room for growth on the world market for pork meat. Canada will soon be 50 percent export dependent," Canada Pork International president Jim Morris told reporters after speaking at the Canadian Wheat Board's annual Grain World meeting.
Canada is about 35 percent export dependent now. Japan, Korea and Hong Kong were among the growth markets, he said.
Canadian pork exports in 1996 set a record at 352,688 tonnes, up 14 percent in value at C$1.105 billion and up 3.3 percent in tonnage, Morris said.
When live hog exports are added to the total, Canadian pork export revenue amounted to C$1.4 billion last year, he said.

"The application of top pig genetics for quality means Manitoba's index for quality is much superior to any of the other provinces and is certainly a major factor in the export of feeders and slaughter pigs to the United States," Cam Brown, a livestock consultant, said at the meeting.
The U.S. bought 35 percent of Canada's 1996 pork exports.
"Americans like our quality, they're disease-free and this is a major demand factor for Manitoba pigs," Brown said.
Forty percent of Manitoba pork exports were destined for the U.S. last year, Manitoba Agriculture statistics show.

"We've got opportunities in Japan and elsewhere where we can talk about the quality that goes into the product that we're selling," Fletcher's Fine Foods Ltd vice president Greg Whalley told delegates.
Fletcher's launched a C$23 million expansion of its processing plant in Red Deer, Alberta, last year to double its kill capacity with a view to supplying the Pacific Rim.
Schneider Corp began a C$40 million expansion of its Winnipeg facility last June to ship chilled pork to Japan.

Canada's largest food processor, Maple Leaf Foods Inc, bought Winnipeg's largest pork packer last fall and plans to build a new facility somewhere on the Prairies with a kill capacity of three million hogs a year to supply Asia.
Farmers are also gearing up with the backing of firms like top grain handler Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, which has expanded into hog barns and bought a 35 percent stake in Fletcher's.
Hog barn operators like Manitoba's Elite Swine Inc are expanding as well. Elite plans two new barns for Alberta.

"The only thing I would say is it takes a lot of on-farm capital to expand the industry and that in itself is rather sobering and this industry is cyclical," CPI's Morris said. CPI is a producer-packer export development firm.
The provincial governments of both Manitoba and Alberta ended their hog export monopolies last year to boost output.
Manitoba produced about 3.2 million hogs in 1996 and Alberta produced 2.84 million. Saskatchewan produced about 1.0 million, provincial agriculture departments said.
It would cost C$500 million to add two million more hogs in Alberta, Alberta Pig Company chairman Bryan Perkins said.
"We'll have to seek alternative sources of capital to build the infrastructure because farmers usually use their own savings," Perkins said.

To add one million more hogs in Manitoba, the largest hog producer on the Prairies, would require 300,000 tonnes more feed grain and a C$200 million capital investment at the farm gate, hog marketer Manitoba Pork director Bill Vaags said.
"I can see this industry growing by leaps and bounds. The environmental side will be the biggest challenge," Vaags said.
((Winnipeg bureau 204 947 3548))
